item.title: RAF isoform selectivity of MEK inhibitors and rational design of a covalent ARAF-MEK inhibitor
item.description: Aberrant activation of the RAS/RAF/mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK)/extracellular signal–regulated kinase pathway is a frequent cause of cancer. Allosteric MEK inhibitors block this pathway by binding RAF-MEK complexes to prevent activation of MEK by RAF. However, how MEK inhibitor potency varies across the three RAF isoforms remains poorly understood. We profiled seven allosteric MEK inhibitors and observed a notable hierarchy of sensitivity: All most potently inhibited CRAF-driven MEK activation while relatively sparing ARAF-driven activation. We identified point mutations in ARAF and CRAF proximate to the MEK inhibitor binding site that markedly altered inhibitor sensitivity. Using a rational design approach, we developed a more potent inhibitor of ARAF-driven MEK signaling, TWG-07-148. Our cryo–electron microscopy structure shows how this acrylamide-containing analog of MEK inhibitor trametinib covalently targets Cys 514 , a residue unique to ARAF. Our studies highlight the importance of the activating RAF isoform as a determinant of MEK inhibitor sensitivity and provide proof of concept for the development of MEK inhibitors that more effectively block ARAF-driven MEK signaling via covalent targeting of Cys 514 .

item.title: Structural basis for start codon selection by eIF5-mimic proteins
item.description: Start codon selection extensively regulates the cellular proteome and is implicated in cancer and other diseases. The eIF5-mimic proteins (5MPs: 5MP1/BZW2 and 5MP2/BZW2) restrict non-AUG start codon usage and thereby reprogram proteoform expression from mRNAs with alternative start sites, such as the oncogenic c-Myc. Here, using in extracto cryo–electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and biochemical assays, we report how 5MP represses translation dependent on the sequence context at start codons. Cryo-EM structures of 48 S preinitiation complexes (PICs) reveal 5MP1 bound at the A site of the small ribosomal subunit. 5MPs act as initiation factors that stabilize an open PIC conformation, promoting mRNA scanning and inhibiting initiation at suboptimal start codons. We propose to designate 5MP as eIF1S (eukaryotic initiation factor 1 scanning). These findings reveal the structural basis for proteome modulation by 5MPs and may help correct dysregulated translation in disease.

item.title: CCAN forms the spherical shell-like structure in interphase kinetochores
item.description: The kinetochore is an essential structure for the faithful chromosome segregation during mitosis. The 16-protein complex known as the constitutive centromere-associated network (CCAN) localizes the centromere throughout the cell cycle and forms the basis of the kinetochore. Although cryo-electron microscopy has provided a structural model of an individual CCAN unit, how multiple CCAN units are organized within cells remains unclear. Here, using in silico and in vivo analyses, we demonstrate that multiple CCAN units form a spherical shell-like structure in interphase DT40 kinetochores. CENP-T and CENP-N localize to the CCAN shell, whereas the CENP-C cupin domain clusters at the center. Molecular dynamics simulations of CCAN assembly suggest that CENP-C-DNA interactions constrain the orientation of CCAN units, supporting a spherical shell-like organization via CENP-C oligomerization. Super-resolution imaging reveals the spherical shell-like structure at DT40 kinetochores, and CENP-C knockout or expression of a CENP-C DNA binding deficient mutant abolishes the structure, consistent with the simulation-derived model. These findings provide important insights into the spatial organization of functional kinetochores within cells.

item.title: Multiple allosteric sites allow for synergistic enhancement of GPCR signaling
item.description: Allosteric modulation of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) offers promising therapeutic opportunities. Although multiple allosteric binding sites have been identified in GPCRs, whether and how these spatially distinct sites cooperate to regulate receptor activation remain poorly understood. Here, we elucidate the molecular mechanism of cooperative multisite allostery in the dopamine D1 receptor (D1R). We developed two novel D1R positive allosteric modulators (PAMs), UNC9815 and UNC10062, and used cryo-electron microscopy to structurally identify two previously uncharacterized D1R allosteric sites occupied by UNC9815/UNC10062 and another D1R PAM, BMS-A1. Both sites localize to the transmembrane helix (TM) 1 to 7 interface as vertically adjacent allosteric pockets organized in a spatially complementary manner. Our structures demonstrate the simultaneous binding of the chemically distinct PAMs (LY3154207, BMS-A1, and UNC9815/UNC10062) in three nonoverlapping pockets. Concurrent engagement of all three allosteric sites produces pronounced functional cooperativity, increasing dopamine potency by >1000-fold, thereby demonstrating that coordinated multisite modulation can achieve substantial pharmacological amplification beyond the limits imposed by single PAM administration. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed that multisite PAM engagement restricts intracellular loop 3 dynamics and stabilizes the TM7-NPxxY activation motif, effects not achieved by binding of LY3154207 alone, thereby biasing the receptor toward a more stabilized active conformation, and may also improve agonist potency by stabilizing extracellular loop 2. Together, these findings establish the structural framework for cooperative multisite allostery in a GPCR, revealing how distributed allosteric sites act in concert to amplify receptor activation and providing a conceptual foundation for developing innovative GPCR allosteric therapeutics.

item.title: SPRIZ (CCDC127) protein conserved in deuterostome animals is a rigid OMM–IMM tether that locally sets mitochondrial IMS volume
item.description: The double-membrane nature of mitochondria generates an intermembrane volume through which ions, reactive oxygen species, and metabolites must flux to reach the matrix or cytosol, but whether this volume is a genetically specified structure remains unknown. We identify SPRIZ (spatial regulator of the intermembrane zone), the product of Ccdc127 , a gene conserved across deuterostome animals. SPRIZ assembles into an ∼18-nanometer homodimeric tether anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) and inserted into the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) through vertebrate-specific hydrophobic loops, physically spacing the two membranes and setting local intermembrane volume. Cryo-electron tomography of native mitochondria revealed rod-like densities spanning the intermembrane space (IMS), consistent with SPRIZ’s predicted rigid coiled-coil architecture and membrane-spanning topology. In mouse liver, two-dimensional morphometry measured ∼3-fold expansion of IMS area with SPRIZ and ∼5.5-fold with lengthened mitochondrial artificial increaser of the IMS (MARTINI); 3D electron tomography confirmed MARTINI’s greater OMM–IMM separation and normalized IMS volume. This expansion was functionally validated by increased 14 C-mannitol accessibility to the IMS and by impaired mitochondrial Ca 2+ uptake. Constitutive Ccdc127/SPRIZ knockout produced viable mice and, in liver mitochondria, preserved overall ultrastructure but caused modest IMS expansion, consistent with loss of local OMM–IMM constraints that stabilize membrane geometry at discrete sites. We therefore identify IMS volume as a genetically encoded and tunable architectural parameter of vertebrate mitochondria. In this model, SPRIZ is a molecular spacing system that locally sets OMM–IMM separation, shaping the environment through which metabolites, ions, and signals diffuse and establishing local gradients within the IMS.

item.title: Atomic structure and dynamics of the mechanosensitive channel MscL from Escherichia coli by cryo-EM and solid-state NMR
item.description: Mechanosensitive channels are central to cellular responses to membrane tension, yet the structural basis of their gating remains incompletely understood. Here, we determine the structures of wild-type and Gly22→Ser (G22S) mutants of MscL from Escherichia coli ( Ec MscL) by cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) in peptide-based lipid nanodiscs and complement them with solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) measurements in liposomes to capture their dynamics in a native-like membrane environment. The cryo-EM structures reveal a closed conformation, whereas analysis of the low-threshold G22S mutant by NMR uncovers widespread conformational changes in both cytoplasmic and periplasmic regions. These data indicate enhanced dynamics and conformational heterogeneity in the mutant, revealing the early transitions from the closed toward the open state. Together, our results establish a synergistic framework integrating cryo-EM and NMR to resolve both structure and dynamics of mechanosensitive channels, and identify lipid-protein interactions as key determinants of MscL gating and mechanosensitivity. Our study further provides a quantitative benchmark for computational investigations of mechanogating and lays the foundation for the rational design of channels with tunable gating kinetics.

item.title: Transposon end recognition and pairing by I-F3 CRISPR-associated transposase
item.description: (Tn7)-like transposons typically contain asymmetric left- and right-end sequences that flank and define DNA cargo. However, how the transposase recognizes these different sequences and assembles them into a catalytically competent state for cut-and-paste transposition remains unknown. Here, we present the cryo-electron microscopy structure of the VchCAST transposase TnsB in complex with transposon DNA ends and host factor IHF, along with biochemistry, molecular dynamics, and in vivo analyses. Our structure reveals the stoichiometry and architecture of the assembly, as well as the DNA distortions required to accommodate transposon end asymmetry. Molecular dynamics suggests that these distortions are required for the coordinated assembly of the complex. Physical association of asymmetric left and right ends results in a previously uncharacterized protein-protein interface that is required for transposition efficiency. Our findings explain how transposases regulate the pairing of transposon end sequences for high-fidelity recognition, reveal a model of transposon-end synapsis, and suggest future avenues to engineer DNA cargo for genome-editing applications.
